Modern language models did not appear in a single leap. They emerged from a sequence of ideas about how a neural network should read, remember, and generate a sequence. Recurrent neural networks introduced a persistent hidden state. Long short-term memory networks made that state easier to train over long distances. Attention let a decoder look back at the most relevant parts of an input. Although the attention mechanism predates Transformers, [*Attention Is All You Need*](https://papers.neurips.cc/paper/7181-attention-is-all-you-need.pdf) [@vaswani2017attention] made attention—not recurrence—the main computational primitive of the Transformer architecture.

::: {.callout-note}
## From recurrence to attention

The progression was gradual rather than a single jump. Simple recurrent cells came first, then gated recurrent cells such as LSTMs and GRUs. Attention moved into recurrent encoder–decoder systems next, letting a decoder look back over all encoder states. Transformers then removed recurrence from the core sequence model and made attention the main primitive.
:::

## Learning objectives

By the end of this lecture, you should be able to:

1. explain why recurrent sequence models were difficult to scale;
2. describe the encoder–decoder Transformer used for translation;
3. explain shifted targets, causal masking, and teacher forcing;
4. distinguish encoder-only, decoder-only, and encoder–decoder Transformers; and
5. match each architecture family to the tasks it naturally supports.

## Before Transformers: recurrence and memory

A basic RNN reads a sequence one token at a time. At position $t$, it combines the current input $x_t$ with the previous hidden state $h_{t-1}$:

$$
h_t = f(x_t, h_{t-1}).
$$

This recurrence gives the model a memory, but it also creates two problems. First, information and gradients must travel through many sequential steps, which makes long-range dependencies difficult to learn. Second, token $t+1$ cannot be processed until token $t$ is complete, limiting parallelism during training.

[Long short-term memory](https://doi.org/10.1162/neco.1997.9.8.1735) [@hochreiter1997lstm] introduced gated memory cells to improve gradient flow and preserve useful information across longer time spans. LSTMs became a standard building block for sequence modeling, including machine translation.

### The recurrent encoder–decoder

In early neural machine translation, an encoder LSTM read the source sentence and compressed it into a fixed-dimensional representation. A decoder LSTM then generated the target sentence one token at a time. The influential [sequence-to-sequence model](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2014/hash/5a18e133cbf9f257297f410bb7eca942-Abstract.html) [@sutskever2014seq2seq] used a deep LSTM encoder and a deep LSTM decoder, reaching 34.8 [BLEU](https://aclanthology.org/P02-1040/) [@papineni2002bleu] on its WMT 2014 English-to-French setup.

::: {.paper-author-note}
\* [Ilya Sutskever on X/Twitter (\@ilyasut)](https://x.com/ilyasut)
:::

Compressing an entire sentence into one fixed vector created an information bottleneck, especially for long sequences. [Bahdanau attention](https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.0473) [@bahdanau2015attention] changed this: at each output step, the decoder could compute a weighted combination of all encoder states rather than relying on only one final vector.

Attention was initially an addition to recurrence. The next step was to ask whether recurrence was needed at all.

## Attention becomes the architecture

The 2017 paper [*Attention Is All You Need*](https://papers.neurips.cc/paper/7181-attention-is-all-you-need.pdf) [@vaswani2017attention] introduced the Transformer for sequence transduction, evaluated primarily on machine translation. Its key move was to replace recurrent and convolutional sequence layers with stacked attention and feed-forward layers.

Because all source positions can be processed together during training, the Transformer is substantially more parallelizable than an RNN. Self-attention also gives every token a short path to every other token: a token can directly attend to a distant token instead of passing information through every intermediate recurrent step.

## How the original Transformer translates

The original Transformer is an **encoder–decoder** model. Unlike the earlier [sequence-to-sequence LSTM](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2014/hash/5a18e133cbf9f257297f410bb7eca942-Abstract.html) [@sutskever2014seq2seq], which passed a single fixed-size encoded state to the decoder, the Transformer encoder produces a **sequence of contextual vectors—one per source token**. Stacked together, these vectors form a matrix often called the encoder memory. At every output step, the decoder uses cross-attention to read across that entire memory.

The encoder returns a matrix of contextual vectors—not one sentence vector. The decoder combines that full encoder memory with the target prefix to predict the next token.

### 1. The encoder reads the source

The source sentence is tokenized. Token embeddings are combined with positional information, then passed through a stack of encoder blocks. Each block uses bidirectional self-attention: every source position may attend to every other source position. The output is a sequence of context-sensitive vectors.

### 2. The decoder reads a shifted target prefix

The decoder starts with a beginning-of-sequence token. During training, it receives the correct target sentence shifted one position to the right:

<pre class="sequence-example" aria-label="The decoder input is beginning-of-sequence, I, am, a. The prediction and training target end with student."><code>Decoder input:    &lt;BOS&gt;  I      am       a
Prediction:        I     am     a        <mark>student</mark>
Training target:   I     am     a        student</code></pre>

At each position, cross-entropy uses the probability assigned to the correct target. If the model predicts **human** instead of **student**, the same idea looks like this:

<pre class="sequence-example" aria-label="At position t, the model predicts human instead of the correct target student, and cross-entropy uses the probability assigned to student. At position t plus one, teacher forcing supplies the correct decoder input and the model predicts today."><code><span class="sequence-label">Position t</span>
Decoder input:     &lt;BOS&gt; I am a
Top prediction:    <mark class="wrong-word">human</mark>
Correct target:    <mark>student</mark>
p(student):        0.08
Cross-entropy:     −ln(0.08) = 2.53

<span class="sequence-label">Position t + 1</span>
Decoder input:     &lt;BOS&gt; I am a student
Top prediction:    today
Correct target:    today
p(today):          0.71
Cross-entropy:     −ln(0.71) = 0.34</code></pre>

This is **teacher forcing**: the decoder input at position $t+1$ is built from the correct target prefix. Training therefore supplies `<BOS> I am a student`, even though the model predicted **human** at position $t$. The model then predicts **today** from that correct prefix.

### 3. A causal mask prevents cheating

The decoder's self-attention is causally masked. When predicting position $i$, it may attend only to target positions before $i$. It cannot inspect the token it is supposed to predict or any later target token.

### 4. Cross-attention connects decoder and encoder

In each decoder block, cross-attention uses the decoder state as a query and the encoder outputs as keys and values. This lets the decoder focus on the relevant source positions for each generated target token.

### 5. Training and inference feed the decoder differently

Both modes receive the same source sentence and keep its encoder memory available to the decoder. The only difference is where the decoder prefix comes from:

<pre class="sequence-example" aria-label="During both training and inference, the source sentence is encoded into the same encoder memory. The table compares decoder inputs and predictions for training and inference."><code><span class="sequence-label">Both modes</span>
Source:           je suis étudiant
Encoder memory:   z₁  z₂  z₃

<span class="sequence-label">Training — decoder input comes from the target</span>
Decoder input                       Predicts
&lt;BOS&gt; I am a student                I am a student today

<span class="sequence-label">Inference — decoder input comes from the model</span>
                  Decoder input      Predicts
Step 1:           &lt;BOS&gt;              I
Step 2:           &lt;BOS&gt; I            am
Step 3:           &lt;BOS&gt; I am         a
Step 4:           &lt;BOS&gt; I am a       student</code></pre>

### Encoder-only: BERT and RoBERTa

[BERT](https://aclanthology.org/N19-1423/) [@devlin2019bert] pre-trains a bidirectional Transformer encoder with a masked-language-model objective: selected input tokens are hidden and the model predicts them using context from both sides. [RoBERTa](https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.11692) [@liu2019roberta] retains the encoder-only structure while revising BERT's training recipe, data, and masking strategy.

Encoder-only models are natural choices for tasks that require understanding or labeling an existing input:

- document or sentence classification, such as sentiment or topic classification;
- token classification, such as named-entity recognition;
- extractive question answering, where the answer is a span in a passage;
- natural-language inference and semantic similarity;
- retrieval and embedding-based similarity, usually with task-specific training; and
- filling masked tokens during pre-training.

They are not naturally designed for long, autoregressive free-form generation because they do not contain a causal generation decoder.

### Decoder-only: GPT-1, GPT-2, and GPT-3

[GPT-1](https://cdn.openai.com/research-covers/language-unsupervised/language_understanding_paper.pdf) [@radford2018gpt], [GPT-2](https://cdn.openai.com/better-language-models/language_models_are_unsupervised_multitask_learners.pdf) [@radford2019gpt2], and [GPT-3](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2020/hash/1457c0d6bfcb4967418bfb8ac142f64a-Abstract.html) [@brown2020gpt3] use a causal Transformer decoder trained to predict the next token.

Decoder-only models naturally support:

- text completion and open-ended generation;
- conditional generation from a textual prompt;
- summarization, translation, and question answering when expressed as prompted generation;
- zero-shot, one-shot, and few-shot task learning;
- classification or structured prediction when formulated through prompting or fine-tuning.

Classification is possible, but **generation is the native training interface**: the model always predicts what token comes next.

### Encoder–decoder: BART and T5

[BART](https://aclanthology.org/2020.acl-main.703/) [@lewis2020bart] and [T5](https://jmlr.org/papers/v21/20-074.html) [@raffel2020t5] are encoder–decoder models, like the original Transformer. BART learns to reconstruct clean text from corrupted input; T5 casts many NLP problems into a unified text-to-text format.

Encoder–decoder models are especially natural for tasks where a distinct input is transformed into a distinct output:

- machine translation;
- abstractive summarization;
- generative question answering;
- paraphrasing and grammatical correction;
- data-to-text generation; and
- other conditional sequence-to-sequence tasks.

## What to remember

1. **LSTM is an RNN architecture.** Gating helped recurrent models learn longer dependencies, but computation remained sequential.
2. **Attention weakened the fixed-vector bottleneck.** A decoder could access all encoder states dynamically.
3. **The Transformer removed recurrence from the core architecture.** This improved parallelism and performed strongly on translation.
4. **Training the decoder uses shifted targets and a causal mask.** The correct prefix is visible; the current and future answers are not.
5. **Architecture determines the natural interface.** Encoders represent inputs, decoders generate continuations, and encoder–decoders transform one sequence into another.
